questions.title: Can a court decide fair use on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, and what materials can it consider?
questions.question_body: The panel affirms dismissal at the pleading stage based on fair use, citing TCA Television and noting it need only consider "the original version of the videos and the JKL segments," plus it takes judicial notice of copyright registrations. At Rule 12(b)(6), I thought the court is limited to the complaint, its exhibits, and documents incorporated by reference (DiFolco). Are courts allowed to watch and compare videos that aren’t attached to the complaint if they are central to the claims? Does the "incorporation by reference" or "integral to the complaint" doctrine typically cover both the original and the allegedly infringing works in copyright cases? And are there limits (e.g., plaintiff disputes authenticity/completeness) that would push this beyond 12(b)(6) into summary judgment territory?

questions.title: How does the "reasonable observer" test for transformative purpose fit with the Supreme Court’s Warhol decision?
questions.question_body: The panel says the transformative analysis turns on what a reasonable observer would think, not the subjective intent of either party, and cites Warhol (2023) for the proposition that subjective intent doesn’t control. But Warhol also emphasized analyzing the specific use’s purpose in relation to the relevant licensing market rather than relying solely on new meaning or message. Here, the court frames Kimmel’s use as commentary about Santos’s willingness to say absurd things for money. How does that square with Warhol’s market-focused approach to factor one? In practice, after Warhol, should courts also assess whether the defendant’s use serves the same or different licensing markets even when the message is clearly critical/commentary? What kinds of allegations or evidence would matter at 12(b)(6)?

questions.title: Does deception in acquiring a work (fake names on Cameo) defeat a fair use defense?
questions.question_body: Santos argued Kimmel’s false identities on Cameo show bad faith that should negate fair use, pointing to Harper & Row’s statement that fair use presupposes good faith. The panel responds that the Supreme Court has "distanced itself" from that statement and emphasizes the critical/commentary purpose instead. What is the current role of "good faith" in fair use after Harper & Row and Campbell? Can deceptive acquisition weigh against fair use under factor one, or is it largely irrelevant unless it ties to market substitution or another factor? Are there cases where a defendant lied to obtain a copy but still prevailed (or lost) on fair use that help clarify how courts treat bad faith in the analysis?

questions.title: Why did the fraudulent inducement claim fail for lack of "out-of-pocket" loss under New York law?
questions.question_body: The panel (citing Lama Holding and Connaughton) says Santos did not allege any out-of-pocket loss, so his fraudulent inducement claim fails. I’m struggling with what counts here: Santos spent time recording the videos, claims reputational harm, and says the broadcast deprived him of licensing value. Why aren’t those cognizable damages? Is the problem that time spent and reputational/expectancy harms are "benefit-of-the-bargain" or consequential rather than out-of-pocket? Could production costs, opportunity costs, or foregone alternative Cameo bookings ever qualify as out-of-pocket losses for a fraud claim in this context? What would a sufficient damages pleading look like under NY law?

questions.title: How did the court evaluate market harm when there might be a market to license these exact Cameo videos to television shows?
questions.question_body: On factor four, the panel quotes Hachette and Campbell to say the question is usurpation of the market (offering a competing substitute) rather than devaluation by criticism, and notes creators typically won’t license lampoons. But here, Kimmel aired the videos themselves on national TV—couldn’t there be a market to license Santos’s Cameo videos (or similar personalized videos) to broadcasters, apart from a market for critical commentary? How do courts distinguish usurpation from mere devaluation when the secondary user shows the complete work to a mass audience? Does the fact that Santos likely wouldn’t have licensed the videos for mocking use end the inquiry, or does a broader market for non-critical broadcast uses matter under factor four?

questions.title: Why didn’t the court resolve Copyright Act preemption of the contract claims, and when are contract/fraud claims preempted under § 301?
questions.question_body: The district court dismissed the breach-of-contract and implied-contract claims as preempted, but the Second Circuit didn’t reach preemption and instead held the claims fail under state law. Doctrinally, when would claims like breach of a platform’s Terms of Service or implied-in-fact promises be preempted by § 301? What is the Second Circuit’s two-prong test (subject matter + equivalence), and how do "extra elements" (like a promise or misrepresentation) affect preemption for contract and fraud claims? If Santos had adequately alleged an implied promise restricting broadcast use, would that kind of undertaking normally avoid preemption as qualitatively different from a copyright claim?

questions.title: What would Santos need to plead to state an implied-in-fact contract under New York law in this scenario?
questions.question_body: The panel says Santos didn’t allege the essential terms or a meeting of the minds that Kimmel would adhere to the Terms of Service or otherwise limit use of the videos. In the context of a buyer requesting a personalized video and the creator supplying it, what facts would plausibly show an implied-in-fact agreement between those two parties (separate from the platform’s user agreement) restricting downstream broadcast or redistribution (e.g., express messages between the parties, standardized creator terms displayed at purchase, industry customs)? Are there New York cases recognizing implied limits on use in similar creative-services transactions that could guide how to plead the essential terms and mutual assent?

questions.title: Under Illinois law, what contract language is needed to make a non-user creator like Santos a third-party beneficiary of Cameo’s Terms of Service?
questions.question_body: The panel applies Illinois law (per the ToS) and emphasizes the strong presumption against third-party beneficiaries absent language “practically an express declaration.” If the ToS contains provisions that appear designed to protect creators (e.g., restrictions on impersonation or redistribution), but don’t explicitly confer enforcement rights on creators, is that ever enough under Illinois law? How explicit does the ToS need to be to let creators sue users as intended beneficiaries, and do courts draw a negative inference when some clauses expressly name third-party beneficiaries but the clauses at issue do not? Any Illinois cases where a platform’s non-signatory service provider was deemed an intended beneficiary of a user agreement?
